answers.l: Snapshots the index. Each commit points to a tree, its parents and an author.
--force-with-lease is the polite version of --force.
fetch, then merge. Or rebase, if you set pull.rebase.
"git add -p" stages changes hunk by hunk.
Copies a repository with its full history. --depth 1 when you don’t need it.
The command you run between every other command.
Joins histories, fast-forwarding when it can.
Replays your commits onto a new base. Rewrites history, so mind shared branches.
Did too many jobs. Git 2.23 split it into switch and restore.
A branch is just a 41-byte file holding a commit hash and a newline.
"git log --graph --oneline --all" draws the subway map.
Working tree versus index by default. --staged for index versus HEAD.
Downloads without touching your working tree.
Since Git 2.28 you can set init.defaultBranch.
A stack of work-in-progress commits hiding in refs/stash.
--soft, --mixed, --hard: how much of your work survives.
Undoes a commit by adding a new one. Safe on shared history.
Copies one commit’s changes onto your branch.
Annotated tags are real objects. Lightweight tags are just refs.
"git blame -w -C" ignores whitespace and follows code that moved.
Added in 2.23 to take branch switching off checkout’s hands.
Added in 2.23 to take file restoring off checkout’s hands.
Shows any object: commit, tree, blob or tag.
Manages the names you push to and fetch from.
Three levels: system, global and local.
Removes from the index and the working tree. --cached keeps the file.
Binary search through history for the commit that broke it. "git bisect run" automates it.
Where "lost" commits are found. Your local undo history.
Check out several branches at once, in separate directories.
Repositories inside repositories. Beloved by nobody.
Searches tracked files, fast.
Git doesn’t track renames. It infers them from content similarity.
Deletes untracked files. Run it with -n first, always.
Applies a diff without committing.
"git help -g" lists the concept guides.
Summarizes commits by author. Release notes in one command.
Names a commit relative to the nearest tag, like v2.1-14-gabc1234.
Exports a tree as tar or zip, without .git.
A whole repository in one file. Sneakernet-friendly.
Checks the object database for corruption.
Packs loose objects and prunes unreachable ones.
Removes unreachable objects.
Applies patches from a mailbox. How the Linux kernel takes contributions.
Turns commits into emails, ready for git am.
Mails patches directly. Still the kernel workflow.
Check out only part of a huge repository.
Merges another repository’s history into a subdirectory.
"git cat-file -p HEAD" shows a commit for what it really is: a few lines of text.
Lists what is in the index.
Turns any ref expression into a hash. The plumbing behind countless scripts.
Rewrites all history. Its own docs now recommend git filter-repo instead.
Yes, git ships with a Tk GUI.
Compares two versions of a patch series. Great for reviewing a force-push.
"Reuse recorded resolution." Remembers how you resolved a conflict and does it again.
Attaches metadata to commits without changing their hashes.
Swaps one object for another everywhere, without rewriting history.
Computes an object ID, and optionally writes the object.
Lists the contents of a tree object.
Finds the best common ancestor of two commits.
Names a commit by its distance from a ref.
An older cousin of git log.
Lists commits not yet upstream. Not to be confused with cherry-pick.
Starts gitweb for your repository in one command.
Writes a pull request for email, years before GitHub.
Schedules background gc, prefetch and commit-graph updates.
Checks a commit’s GPG or SSH signature.
Home of --assume-unchanged and --skip-worktree.
Collects system details for a bug report. Added in 2.27.
The engine behind most repository converters.
A graphical commit tool.
